example.fact: Ji Kang, one of the celebrated 'Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove,' was a philosopher, poet, and musician executed for his political defiance in 262 CE — legend says he calmly played the guqin piece 广陵散 just before his execution.

components.note: 土 (earth, soil) — 圪 appears mainly in dialectal place names and words from the Shanxi region.
乞 (qǐ) no longer resembles 圪's modern reading gē — the sound has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 圪这个字常出现在山西方言的地名里。
example.pinyin: Gē zhège zì cháng chūxiàn zài Shānxī fāngyán de dìmíng lǐ.
example.english: The character 'ge' often appears in place names in the Shanxi dialect.
example.fact: 圪 is a character used almost purely for its sound, common in place names and dialect words from Shanxi and Shaanxi provinces, such as 圪塔 (gēda, 'lump, knot').

meanings: hair rolled up in a bun
hair rolled up in a bun, topknot

components.note: 髟 (long, flowing hair) — 髻 names a bun or knot of hair.
吉 (jí) is close to 髻's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 古代女子常将头发梳成发髻。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài nǚzǐ cháng jiāng tóufa shū chéng fàjì.
example.english: Women in ancient times often combed their hair into a bun.
example.fact: The style and position of a hair bun in ancient China often signaled a woman's marital status, age, or social rank — married women, for instance, typically wore their hair up, while unmarried girls commonly kept it in braids.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗬 is a pure exclamation of surprise.
荷 (hé) is close to 嗬's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 嗬!这么大的南瓜,真是罕见。
example.pinyin: Hē! Zhème dà de nánguā, zhēnshi hǎnjiàn.
example.english: Wow! Such a huge pumpkin — that's really rare.
example.fact: 嗬 is a pure interjection, one of a set of mouth-radical characters in Chinese (like 啊, 哦, 咦) created specifically to write down spoken exclamations that carry no meaning beyond the emotion of the moment.

components.note: 车 (cart, vehicle) — 辎 names a covered supply cart or wagon.
甾 (zāi) shares 辎's initial sound but not the full syllable — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 古代行军作战,辎重的运输十分重要。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài xíngjūn zuòzhàn, zīzhòng de yùnshū shífēn zhòngyào.
example.english: In ancient military campaigns, transporting supplies was extremely important.
example.fact: 辎重 (zīzhòng) named an army's baggage train of supply wagons — protecting or capturing the enemy's 辎重 was a recurring strategic objective described throughout classical Chinese military texts like Sun Tzu's Art of War.

etymologyHint: The mark 志 of an illness 疒; 志 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 疒 (sickness, ailment) — used broadly here for marks or blemishes on the body, including moles.
志 (zhì) is an exact match for 痣's reading — 志 itself means 'mark, sign,' fitting for a mole or birthmark.

example.hanzi: 她脸上有一颗小痣,很有特色。
example.pinyin: Tā liǎn shàng yǒu yì kē xiǎo zhì, hěn yǒu tèsè.
example.english: She has a small mole on her face that's quite distinctive.
example.fact: In traditional Chinese physiognomy (面相学), the position of a mole on someone's face was often read as an omen about their fortune or character — a superstition still occasionally referenced in fortune-telling and popular culture today.

meanings: to give birth to a child

components.note: 女 (woman) — 娩 describes the act of giving birth.
免 (miǎn) gives an exact match for 娩's reading.

example.hanzi: 她将在下个月分娩。
example.pinyin: Tā jiāng zài xià gè yuè fēnmiǎn.
example.english: She will give birth next month.
example.fact: 分娩 (fēnmiǎn) is the standard clinical Chinese term for childbirth, used in hospitals and medical documents, distinct from the more casual, everyday phrase 生孩子 ('to have a baby').

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — 谄 describes flattering, insincere speech.
臽 (xiàn) no longer resembles 谄's modern reading chǎn — the sound has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 他总是谄媚上司,想尽办法讨好领导。
example.pinyin: Tā zǒngshì chǎnmèi shàngsi, xiǎng jìn bànfǎ tǎohǎo lǐngdǎo.
example.english: He always flatters his boss, trying every way to please his superiors.
example.fact: 谄媚 (chǎnmèi) carries a strongly negative connotation in Chinese, describing insincere, servile flattery aimed purely at personal gain — distinct from sincere compliments or polite praise.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蛐 names the cricket, in the colloquial term 蛐蛐.
曲 (qū) gives an exact match for 蛐's reading.

example.hanzi: 北京的老人喜欢养蛐蛐当宠物。
example.pinyin: Běijīng de lǎorén xǐhuan yǎng qūqu dāng chǒngwù.
example.english: Old folks in Beijing like keeping crickets as pets.
example.fact: Cricket-keeping and cricket-fighting has been a popular pastime in Beijing and other northern Chinese cities for centuries, with fighting crickets sometimes fetching high prices from serious collectors.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹞 names a small, agile bird of prey, the sparrow hawk.

example.hanzi: 鹞是一种体型较小但敏捷凶猛的猛禽。
example.pinyin: Yào shì yì zhǒng tǐxíng jiào xiǎo dàn mǐnjié xiōngměng de měngqín.
example.english: The sparrow hawk is a bird of prey that's relatively small but agile and fierce.
example.fact: 鹞 gave its name to an old regional term for a kite, 纸鹞, because a paper kite darting on the wind reminded people of this swift, agile hawk.

components.note: 羽 (feather, wings) — 翱 describes soaring flight.
皋 (gāo) shares 翱's final sound but not its initial — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 老鹰在天空中自由翱翔。
example.pinyin: Lǎoyīng zài tiānkōng zhōng zìyóu áoxiáng.
example.english: The eagle soars freely through the sky.
example.fact: 翱翔 (áoxiáng) describes soaring, gliding flight and is frequently used figuratively in Chinese for ambition or freedom, as in 在知识的海洋中翱翔 ('to soar through the ocean of knowledge').

components.note: 广 (house, shelter) — 庖 names a kitchen.
包 (bāo) shares 庖's final sound but not its initial — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 《庄子》中庖丁解牛的故事讲述了熟能生巧的道理。
example.pinyin: Zhuāngzǐ zhōng Páodīng jiě niú de gùshi jiǎngshù le shúnéngshēngqiǎo de dàolǐ.
example.english: The story of Cook Ding cutting up an ox in the Zhuangzi illustrates the principle that practice makes perfect.
example.fact: 庖丁解牛 ('Cook Ding cuts up an ox'), a famous parable from the Daoist text Zhuangzi, describes a butcher whose knife skills became so refined through practice that he worked by feel and rhythm alone.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 籁 originally named a bamboo pipe or flute, and by extension any natural sound.
赖 (lài) gives an exact match for 籁's reading.

example.hanzi: 她的歌声被赞誉为天籁之音。
example.pinyin: Tā de gēshēng bèi zànyù wéi tiānlài zhī yīn.
example.english: Her singing voice has been praised as a heavenly, natural sound.
example.fact: 天籁 (tiānlài) originally referred, in the Daoist classic Zhuangzi, to the natural sounds made by wind passing through hollow openings in the earth and trees — today it's a common compliment for an especially pure singing voice.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plants) — 蓿 names a forage plant, alfalfa, in the compound 苜蓿.
宿 (sù) shares 蓿's final sound but not its initial — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 苜蓿是一种常见的牲畜饲料作物。
example.pinyin: Mùxu shì yì zhǒng chángjiàn de shēngchù sìliào zuòwù.
example.english: Alfalfa is a common forage crop for livestock.
example.fact: Alfalfa was introduced to China from Central Asia over 2,000 years ago along the Silk Road, traditionally credited to the Han-dynasty envoy Zhang Qian, who brought back seeds along with grapes and other Western crops.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鳗 names the eel.
曼 (màn) is close to 鳗's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 日本料理中的烤鳗鱼很受欢迎。
example.pinyin: Rìběn liàolǐ zhōng de kǎo mányú hěn shòu huānyíng.
example.english: Grilled eel in Japanese cuisine is very popular.
example.fact: Eels have one of the most mysterious life cycles in the animal kingdom — many species are born far out at sea, migrate thousands of kilometers to freshwater rivers to grow, then return to the ocean to spawn and die.

meanings: used in 瘧子|疟子[yao4 zi5]

components.note: 疒 (sickness, ailment) — 疟 names an infectious disease, malaria.

example.hanzi: 疟疾是一种由蚊子传播的疾病。
example.pinyin: Nüèji shì yì zhǒng yóu wénzi chuánbò de jíbìng.
example.english: Malaria is a disease transmitted by mosquitoes.
example.fact: The 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Chinese scientist Tu Youyou for discovering artemisinin (青蒿素), a malaria treatment derived from sweet wormwood that has saved millions of lives worldwide.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲇 names the catfish.
占 (zhàn) no longer resembles 鲇's modern reading nián — the sound has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 鲇鱼的皮肤光滑,没有鱼鳞。
example.pinyin: Niányú de pífū guānghuá, méiyǒu yúlín.
example.english: Catfish have smooth skin without scales.
example.fact: 鲇鱼效应 (the 'catfish effect') is a popular Chinese business metaphor describing how introducing one aggressive, disruptive competitor into a stagnant market or team can spur everyone else into more active performance.

components.note: 言 (words, speech) is assigned as this character's semantic element in its traditional structure, though 這's modern sense as 'this' has drifted from any literal connection to speech.
辶 (chuò, 'to walk') no longer resembles 這's modern reading zhè — the sound has diverged considerably over the character's long history, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 這是我第一次看到繁體字寫的'这'。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ dì yī cì kàndào fántǐzì xiě de 'zhè'.
example.english: This is the first time I've seen the traditional character form of 'this.'
example.fact: 這 is the traditional (unsimplified) form of the extremely common word 这 ('this') — still used today in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau, and in older printed texts from mainland China before the 1950s simplification reforms.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嚅 describes hesitant movement of the mouth or lips while trying to speak.
需 (xū) shares 嚅's final sound but not its initial — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 她张口欲言,却嚅动了几下嘴唇,什么也没说。
example.pinyin: Tā zhāngkǒu yù yán, què rú dòng le jǐ xià zuǐchún, shénme yě méi shuō.
example.english: She opened her mouth as if to speak, but her lips just moved hesitantly, and she said nothing.
example.fact: 嗫 and 嚅 are bound morphemes — characters that carry meaning but, outside a few classical uses, appear in modern Mandarin only paired together as 嗫嚅, never standing alone the way independent words like 走 or 说 can.

components.note: 疒 (sickness, ailment) — 瘀 names internal bleeding or bruising under the skin.
於 (yú) is close to 瘀's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 撞到桌角后,他的腿上出现了一片瘀血。
example.pinyin: Zhuàngdào zhuōjiǎo hòu, tā de tuǐ shàng chūxiàn le yí piàn yūxuè.
example.english: After bumping into the corner of the table, a bruise appeared on his leg.
example.fact: A bruise forms when an impact ruptures small blood vessels under the skin, leaking blood into surrounding tissue — its color changes over about two weeks as the body reabsorbs the trapped blood, cycling through red, purple, green, and yellow.

components.note: 页 (head) — 颔 names the chin, a part of the head.
含 (hán) is close to 颔's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 老师微微颔首,表示同意他的看法。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī wéiwéi hànshǒu, biǎoshì tóngyì tā de kànfǎ.
example.english: The teacher nodded slightly, indicating agreement with his view.
example.fact: 颔首 (hànshǒu, 'to nod') is a more literary, formal way to describe nodding than the everyday 点头, often used in writing to depict a dignified, understated gesture of approval.

components.note: 黑 (black) — 黜 uses the idea of being 'blackened' or disgraced, similar to the English idea of being blacklisted, extended to being dismissed or demoted from office.
出 (chū) is close to 黜's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 汉武帝罢黜百家,独尊儒术。
example.pinyin: Hàn Wǔdì bàchù bǎijiā, dú zūn rúshù.
example.english: Emperor Wu of Han dismissed the hundred schools of thought and elevated Confucianism alone.
example.fact: 罢黜百家,独尊儒术 describes Emperor Wu of Han's policy around 134 BCE that made Confucianism the dominant state ideology, sidelining rival philosophies like Legalism and Daoism for most of imperial Chinese history afterward.

components.note: 黑 (black) — 黠 uses the idea of dark, hidden cunning, similar to how English speakers might call sly scheming 'dark.'
吉 (jí) no longer resembles 黠's modern reading xiá — the sound has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 这只狐狸看起来十分狡黠。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī húli kànqǐlái shífēn jiǎoxiá.
example.english: This fox looks very cunning and sly.
example.fact: 狡黠 (jiǎoxiá) describes clever, sly cunning and is often used for foxes in Chinese fables and idioms, continuing a folklore tradition — shared with many cultures — that casts the fox as the animal kingdom's trickster.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 濑 names a shallow area of swift-flowing water, rapids.
赖 (lài) gives an exact match for 濑's reading.

example.hanzi: 溪流在石头间形成了湍急的浅濑。
example.pinyin: Xīliú zài shítou jiān xíngchéng le tuānjí de qiǎnlài.
example.english: The stream formed swift, shallow rapids among the rocks.
example.fact: A related traditional form of this character also appears in the Japanese place name Seto Inland Sea (瀨戸内海), showing how shared characters can carry related meanings of shallow, swift-moving water across languages.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 馁 originally meant simply hungry or starving, later extended to being discouraged or dispirited.
妥 (tuǒ) no longer resembles 馁's modern reading něi — the sound has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 比赛落后时,队员们并没有气馁。
example.pinyin: Bǐsài luòhòu shí, duìyuánmen bìng méiyǒu qìněi.
example.english: Even while behind in the competition, the team members didn't lose heart.
example.fact: 气馁 (qìněi, 'to lose heart') links being discouraged to being hungry for spirit — 馁 originally meant simply 'hungry, starving,' and the character's food radical 饣 still visibly carries that older, literal sense.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洵 originally could describe a whirlpool, and by extension came to mean something genuine or intensely real.
旬 (xún) gives an exact match for 洵's reading.

example.hanzi: 《诗经》中有'洵美且都'的诗句,赞美女子的美丽。
example.pinyin: Shījīng zhōng yǒu 'xún měi qiě dū' de shījù, zànměi nǚzǐ de měilì.
example.english: The Book of Songs contains the line 'truly beautiful and elegant,' praising a woman's beauty.
example.fact: 洵 is a literary intensifier meaning 'truly, genuinely,' found in classical texts like the Book of Songs (诗经) — in modern Mandarin it survives almost only in formal writing or occasionally as a character in given names.

etymologyHint: A weight on 上 the heart 心

components.note: 上 (above, on top) — depicts something weighing down on top of the heart.
心 (heart) — 忐, used only in 忐忑 ('nervous, uneasy'), relates to an unsettled emotional state.

example.hanzi: 考试成绩还没公布,她心里忐忑不安。
example.pinyin: Kǎoshì chéngjì hái méi gōngbù, tā xīnlǐ tǎntè bù'ān.
example.english: Since her exam results hadn't been announced yet, she felt restless and anxious.
example.fact: 忐 and 忑 are a rare case in Chinese: two characters created purely to visually depict their meaning by stacking 上 and 下 ('above'/'below') over 心 ('heart'), evoking a heart being pushed and pulled.

etymologyHint: A weight under 下 the heart 心

components.note: 下 (below, underneath) — pairs with 忐's 上 to depict a weight pressing from beneath the heart.
心 (heart) — 忑, used only in 忐忑, relates to an unsettled emotional state.

example.hanzi: 他忐忑地打开了考试成绩单。
example.pinyin: Tā tǎntè de dǎkāi le kǎoshì chéngjì dān.
example.english: He nervously opened his exam results.
example.fact: Unlike most two-character Chinese words, where each character can often stand alone with related meaning, 忑 has no independent meaning or usage of its own outside the fixed pair 忐忑 — it exists purely as half of a matched set.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 砥 names a fine-grained whetstone used for sharpening.
氐 (dī) is close to 砥's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 多年的挫折砥砺了他坚强的意志。
example.pinyin: Duōnián de cuòzhé dǐlì le tā jiānqiáng de yìzhì.
example.english: Years of setbacks tempered his strong willpower.
example.fact: 砥砺前行 ('to forge ahead, honed by hardship') became a widely used phrase in Chinese official and media rhetoric in the 2010s, evoking a blade sharpened on a whetstone as a metaphor for character strengthened through difficulty.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咂 describes smacking or clicking sounds made with the mouth, as in tasting.
匝 (zā) gives an exact match for 咂's reading.

example.hanzi: 他吃了一口菜,满意地咂咂嘴。
example.pinyin: Tā chī le yì kǒu cài, mǎnyì de zāzā zuǐ.
example.english: He took a bite of the dish and smacked his lips in satisfaction.
example.fact: 咂嘴 (zāzuǐ, 'to smack one's lips') is a common descriptive gesture in Chinese writing for savoring food, and can also signal thoughtful hesitation, as in 咂嘴沉思 ('smacking one's lips while pondering').

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 罹 describes suffering or sorrow, especially misfortune that befalls someone.

example.hanzi: 这次空难中,机上乘客不幸全部罹难。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì kōngnàn zhōng, jī shàng chéngkè bùxìng quánbù línàn.
example.english: In this plane crash, all the passengers on board tragically perished.
example.fact: 罹难 (línàn) is the standard, somewhat formal term used in Chinese news reports for people who die in disasters, accidents, or attacks — it specifically implies dying through misfortune rather than natural causes.

components.note: 米 (rice, grain) — 糠 names the husks and bran left over from processing grain.
康 (kāng) gives an exact match for 糠's reading.

example.hanzi: '糟糠之妻不下堂'是一句古老的成语。
example.pinyin: 'Zāokāng zhī qī bú xià táng' shì yì jù gǔlǎo de chéngyǔ.
example.english: 'A wife who shared your hardship should not be cast aside' is an old Chinese idiom.
example.fact: 糟糠之妻不下堂 comes from a story about the Han-dynasty official Song Hong, who refused the emperor's suggestion that he divorce his humble wife, replying that a wife who shared his years of poverty should never be abandoned.

meanings: (literary) to encircle; to go around; to surround

example.hanzi: 前方五百米是高速公路的出口匝道。
example.pinyin: Qiánfāng wǔbǎi mǐ shì gāosù gōnglù de chūkǒu zādào.
example.english: 500 meters ahead is the highway's exit ramp.
example.fact: 匝道 (zādào) is the standard Chinese traffic term for the ramps connecting highways to local roads — a modern technical use for a character whose classical meaning was simply 'to encircle' or 'a full circle around.'

components.note: 亻 (person) — 偃 describes a person lying down or ceasing activity.
匽 (yǎn) gives an exact match for 偃's reading.

example.hanzi: 谈判失败后,双方偃旗息鼓,暂时休战。
example.pinyin: Tánpàn shībài hòu, shuāngfāng yǎnqí xīgǔ, zhànshí xiūzhàn.
example.english: After the negotiations failed, both sides quietly stood down and temporarily ceased hostilities.
example.fact: 偃旗息鼓 ('lower the flags, silence the drums') is a military idiom describing a covert retreat or a quiet halt to an activity, since lowering flags and silencing drums would hide an army's movements or signal a stop.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淙 describes the gurgling sound of flowing water.
宗 (zōng) shares 淙's final sound but not its initial — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 泉水淙淙地流下山间。
example.pinyin: Quánshuǐ cóngcóng de liú xià shānjiān.
example.english: The spring water gurgled and flowed down through the mountains.
example.fact: 淙淙 (cóngcóng) is one of several Chinese onomatopoeias for flowing water, alongside 潺潺 (chánchán) and 汩汩 (gǔgǔ) — each capturing a slightly different quality or volume of sound.

etymologyHint: To thread 纟 a needle 刃; 刃 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 纫 describes the action of threading a needle or sewing.
刃 (rèn) is an exact match for 纫's reading — 刃 itself depicts a knife blade, here suggesting the sharp point of a needle.

example.hanzi: 奶奶年轻时用缝纫机做过很多衣服。
example.pinyin: Nǎinai niánqīng shí yòng féngrènjī zuò guò hěn duō yīfu.
example.english: When grandma was young, she made many clothes using a sewing machine.
example.fact: The sewing machine became one of the 'three must-haves' (三大件) for a Chinese household to aspire to in the 1960s-70s, alongside a bicycle and a wristwatch.

meanings: respectful reply of assent to superiors

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喏 is an interjection, either a respectful assent or a word for pointing something out.
若 (ruò) shares 喏's final sound but not its initial — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 他恭敬地应了一声'喏'。
example.pinyin: Tā gōngjìng de yìng le yì shēng 'nuò'.
example.english: He respectfully replied with a 'yes, sir.'
example.fact: 喏 as a respectful assent was historically used when addressing superiors, especially in period dramas depicting imperial court or military scenes, while as a plain interjection it also just means 'here!' or 'look!' when pointing something out.

components.note: 门 (gate, door) — 闾 originally named the gate of a village or residential district.
吕 (lǚ) is close to 闾's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 他晚年退隐回乡,安居闾里。
example.pinyin: Tā wǎnnián tuìyǐn huíxiāng, ānjū lǚlǐ.
example.english: In his later years, he retired to his hometown and settled down in the village.
example.fact: 闾 originally named the communal gate of an ancient residential unit of twenty-five households — the character's meaning gradually broadened from that specific gate to the village or neighborhood itself.

etymologyHint: To banish 去 a spirit 礻; 去 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 礻 (spirit, ritual) — 祛 relates to ritual practices for warding off evil or illness.
去 (qù) is close to 祛's reading qū — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 中医认为薏米有祛湿的功效。
example.pinyin: Zhōngyī rènwéi yìmǐ yǒu qūshī de gōngxiào.
example.english: Traditional Chinese medicine holds that pearl barley has the effect of dispelling dampness.
example.fact: 祛湿 ('dispelling dampness') reflects a core concept in Traditional Chinese Medicine theory, where excess 'dampness' in the body is blamed for symptoms like fatigue and bloating — a concept with no direct equivalent in Western biomedicine but widely referenced in Chinese diet and wellness culture.

components.note: 虫 (insect, worm) — 蛰 describes small creatures lying dormant underground through winter.
执 (zhí) shares 蛰's initial sound but not the full syllable — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 惊蛰是二十四节气中的第三个节气。
example.pinyin: Jīngzhé shì èrshísì jiéqì zhōng de dì sān gè jiéqì.
example.english: Awakening of Insects is the third of the 24 solar terms.
example.fact: 惊蛰 ('Awakening of Insects'), one of China's traditional 24 solar terms marking the agricultural calendar, is named for the belief that spring thunder wakes hibernating insects from their winter dormancy underground.

meanings: used in 靦腆|腼腆[mian3 tian3]

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 腼 relates to one's face or expression, as in a bashful, blushing look.
面 (miàn) is close to 腼's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 这个男孩很腼腆,见到生人就低头不说话。
example.pinyin: Zhège nánhái hěn miǎntiǎn, jiàndào shēngrén jiù dītóu bù shuōhuà.
example.english: This boy is very shy — when he meets strangers, he lowers his head and doesn't speak.
example.fact: 腼腆 (miǎntiǎn) specifically describes a shy, bashful demeanor especially common in describing children or young people who blush or go quiet around new people.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 涝 describes flooding or waterlogging caused by excess rain.
劳 (láo) is close to 涝's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 今年夏天,南方多地遭遇了严重的涝灾。
example.pinyin: Jīnnián xiàtiān, nánfāng duō dì zāoyù le yánzhòng de làozāi.
example.english: This summer, many places in the south suffered severe flooding disasters.
example.fact: 旱涝 ('drought and flood') pairs two opposite agricultural disasters that have long shaped Chinese water management policy, from ancient flood-control projects like the Dujiangyan irrigation system to today's dam and reservoir networks.

meanings: one of the seven planets of pre-modern astronomy (the sun
etymologyHint: A spectacular 翟 star 日; 翟 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 日 (sun) — 曜 relates to brightness and radiance, extended to the sun and other heavenly bodies.
翟 (a long-tailed pheasant with brilliant plumage) reinforces 曜's meaning of brightness and splendor, as in the sun, moon, and stars, together called 七曜 in classical Chinese astronomy.

example.hanzi: 日语的星期几都用'曜日'来表示。
example.pinyin: Rìyǔ de xīngqí jǐ dōu yòng 'yàorì' lái biǎoshì.
example.english: In Japanese, the days of the week are all expressed using 'yōbi' (曜日).
example.fact: Japan still uses this character in 曜日 (yōbi) to name the days of the week — 月曜日 (Monday, 'moon day'), 火曜日 (Tuesday, 'fire day'), and so on — a system borrowed from ancient Chinese astronomy, which grouped the sun, moon, and five visible planets as the seven 曜 ('luminaries').

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or lean-to shelter) — 厩 names an enclosed shelter for animals, a stable.
既 (jì) shares 厩's initial sound but not the full syllable — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 马厩里养着几匹健壮的骏马。
example.pinyin: Mǎjiù lǐ yǎng zhe jǐ pǐ jiànzhuàng de jùnmǎ.
example.english: Several sturdy, fine horses are kept in the stable.
example.fact: Horse stables were of major strategic importance in imperial China, since cavalry and mounted messengers depended on well-maintained government-run horse stations, some forming part of the empire's postal relay system along its northern frontiers.

components.note: 疒 (sickness, ailment) — 疽 names a deep, festering abscess or ulcer.
且 (qiě) no longer resembles 疽's modern reading jū — the sound has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 伤口感染后可能形成疽。
example.pinyin: Shāngkǒu gǎnrǎn hòu kěnéng xíngchéng jū.
example.english: An infected wound can develop into an abscess.
example.fact: 痈疽 (yōngjū) describes a deep, pus-filled abscess; medically, most such abscesses are caused by Staphylococcus bacteria infecting a hair follicle or wound, prompting the body's immune response to wall off the infection with pus.

components.note: 王 (king) — reflects an old ritual in which the king stayed within the gate during an intercalary month, since it fell outside the normal calendar order.
门 (mén) no longer resembles 闰's modern reading rùn — the sound has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally treated as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 今年是闰年,二月有二十九天。
example.pinyin: Jīnnián shì rùnnián, èryuè yǒu èrshíjiǔ tiān.
example.english: This year is a leap year, so February has 29 days.
example.fact: The ancient dictionary Shuowen Jiezi explains 闰's structure as depicting the king remaining inside the gate during an intercalary month, since this extra month fell outside the normal calendar and called for reduced ceremony.

etymologyHint: Swirling 回 water 氵; 回 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洄 describes swirling or circling water, as in an eddy.
回 (huí) is an exact match for 洄's reading — 回 itself means 'to turn, to circle back,' matching the swirling motion of an eddy.

example.hanzi: 每年秋天,鲑鱼都会洄游到出生的河流产卵。
example.pinyin: Měinián qiūtiān, guīyú dōu huì huíyóu dào chūshēng de héliú chǎnluǎn.
example.english: Every autumn, salmon migrate back upstream to the river where they were born to spawn.
example.fact: 洄游 is the standard biological term for migratory behavior like that of salmon, which use a combination of magnetic field sensing and smell to navigate back to the exact river, and sometimes the exact stream, where they hatched years earlier.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 煊 describes warmth.
宣 (xuān) gives an exact match for 煊's reading.

example.hanzi: 煊是暄的异体字,意思是温暖。
example.pinyin: Xuān shì xuān de yìtǐzì, yìsi shì wēnnuǎn.
example.english: Xuan (煊) is a variant form of xuan (暄), meaning warm.
example.fact: 煊 is a rare variant character mostly seen today in given names, chosen for its bright, warm meaning and the auspicious fire radical 火 — variant characters like this often survive in names long after falling out of everyday written use.

etymologyHint: The evening 夕 tide 氵; 夕 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汐 names the tide, specifically the evening ebb tide.
夕 (xī) is an exact match for 汐's reading — 夕 itself means 'evening, dusk,' pinpointing this as the evening tide.

example.hanzi: 潮汐是由月球引力引起的海水周期性涨落。
example.pinyin: Cháoxī shì yóu yuèqiú yǐnlì yǐnqǐ de hǎishuǐ zhōuqīxìng zhǎngluò.
example.english: Tides are the periodic rise and fall of seawater caused by the moon's gravitational pull.
example.fact: Tides are caused mainly by the moon's gravitational pull, with the sun contributing a smaller effect — when the sun and moon align during a new or full moon, their combined pull produces especially large 'spring tides.'

components.note: 艹 (grass, plants) — 藓 names moss.
鲜 (xiān) is close to 藓's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 潮湿的石头上长满了苔藓。
example.pinyin: Cháoshī de shítou shàng zhǎng mǎn le táixiǎn.
example.english: The damp rocks are covered with moss.
example.fact: Mosses lack true roots and vascular tissue, absorbing water directly through their surface — which is why they thrive in damp, shaded spots and were among the very first plants to colonize land, roughly 470 million years ago.

meanings: a semicircular jade ornament used as a pendant

components.note: 王 (here the 玉 radical, 'jade') — 璜 names a semicircular jade ornament.
黄 (huáng) gives an exact match for 璜's reading.

example.hanzi: 考古学家在墓中发现了一件精美的玉璜。
example.pinyin: Kǎogǔ xuéjiā zài mù zhōng fāxiàn le yí jiàn jīngměi de yùhuáng.
example.english: Archaeologists discovered an exquisite semicircular jade pendant in the tomb.
example.fact: 璜 (a semicircular jade pendant) is one of six classical ritual jade shapes described in the Rites of Zhou, alongside the disc-shaped 璧 and cylindrical 琮, each reportedly linked to a different direction or cosmological symbol.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铬 names the metallic element chromium.
各 (gè) gives an exact match for 铬's reading.

example.hanzi: 不锈钢中含有一定比例的铬。
example.pinyin: Bùxiùgāng zhōng hányǒu yídìng bǐlì de gè.
example.english: Stainless steel contains a certain proportion of chromium.
example.fact: Chromium is what makes stainless steel 'stainless' — adding just 10.5% or more chromium to steel causes a thin, invisible layer of chromium oxide to form on the surface, protecting the metal underneath from rust.

components.note: 糹 (thread, silk) — 經 originally named the vertical warp threads on a loom, extended to mean a foundational, 'threaded-through' text.
巠 (jīng) gives an exact match for 經's reading.

example.hanzi: 《易經》是中国最古老的经典之一。
example.pinyin: Yìjīng shì Zhōngguó zuì gǔlǎo de jīngdiǎn zhī yī.
example.english: The Book of Changes is one of China's oldest classic texts.
example.fact: 經 is the traditional form of 经, still used in Taiwan and Hong Kong and in titles like 《易經》(the Book of Changes) — the thread radical reflects the character's original meaning, the warp threads on a loom.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渥 originally described being deeply soaked or moistened, extended to mean generous or abundant.
屋 (wū) shares 渥's initial sound but not the full syllable — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 这份工作待遇优渥,吸引了很多人应聘。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn gōngzuò dàiyù yōuwò, xīyǐn le hěn duō rén yìngpìn.
example.english: This job offers generous benefits, attracting many applicants.
example.fact: 优渥 (yōuwò) extends 渥's older meaning of being richly 'soaked' or saturated into a common modern phrase for generous pay, benefits, or living conditions, as in 待遇优渥.

components.note: 革 (leather, hide) — 靼 originally described softened, tanned leather.
旦 (dàn) shares 靼's initial sound but not the full syllable — only a partial resemblance.

example.hanzi: 靼字本义与皮革有关。
example.pinyin: Dá zì běnyì yǔ pígé yǒuguān.
example.english: The character 'da' originally relates to leather in meaning.
example.fact: On its own, 靼 originally meant softened, tanned leather — it's now seen almost exclusively as the second half of 鞑靼 (Tatar), a case where a character's independent original meaning has been almost entirely displaced by its role in one compound word.

meanings: to become violent under the influence of alcohol
etymologyHint: A dangerous 凶 drunk 酉

components.note: 酉 (wine, alcohol) — 酗 relates to being drunk, as in 酗酒 (xùjiǔ), to drink excessively.
凶 (vicious, ominous) — captures the aggressive or dangerous behavior that can come with drunkenness, as in 酗酒 leading to violence.

example.hanzi: 长期酗酒对身体健康危害很大。
example.pinyin: Chángqī xùjiǔ duì shēntǐ jiànkāng wēihài hěn dà.
example.english: Long-term alcohol abuse is very harmful to physical health.
example.fact: The World Health Organization classifies alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning there is no safe threshold below which drinking carries zero cancer risk — a fact behind many public health campaigns against habitual heavy drinking.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plants) — 苓 names a medicinal fungus, in the compound 茯苓.
令 (lìng) is close to 苓's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 茯苓是中药里常用的一种药材。
example.pinyin: Fúlíng shì zhōngyào lǐ chángyòng de yì zhǒng yàocái.
example.english: Poria fungus is a commonly used ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine.
example.fact: Poria, a fungus that grows on pine tree roots, is one of the most frequently prescribed ingredients in classical Chinese herbal formulas, believed in TCM theory to help drain excess dampness and calm the mind.

etymologyHint: Forbidden 禁 to speak 口; 禁 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 噤 relates to the mouth being shut, unable to speak.
禁 (jìn) is an exact match for 噤's reading — 禁 itself means 'to forbid, to prohibit,' matching the sense of the mouth being forcibly silenced.

example.hanzi: 面对上司的质问,他噤若寒蝉,不敢辩解。
example.pinyin: Miànduì shàngsi de zhìwèn, tā jìn ruò hánchán, bùgǎn biànjiě.
example.english: Facing his boss's questioning, he was silent as a cold cicada, not daring to explain himself.
example.fact: 噤若寒蝉 ('silent as a cicada in the cold') is a vivid idiom for being too frightened to speak, based on the observation that cicadas, which chirp loudly all summer, fall completely silent once cold weather sets in.

meanings: 8 in. length unit of Zhou dynasty

components.note: 尺 (a unit of length; ruler) — 咫 names a short unit of length used in the Zhou dynasty.
只 (zhī) is close to 咫's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 两人近在咫尺,却像隔着千山万水。
example.pinyin: Liǎng rén jìnzài zhǐchǐ, què xiàng gézhe qiānshān wànshuǐ.
example.english: The two of them were within arm's reach, yet it felt as if a thousand mountains and rivers separated them.
example.fact: 咫尺 combines two ancient Zhou-dynasty units of length — 咫 (about 20 cm) and 尺 (about 23 cm) — into an idiom for a very short distance, most often used today in the phrase 近在咫尺 ('so close it's within arm's reach').

components.note: 木 (tree) — 椿 names a tree, the Chinese toon, prized for its edible spring sprouts.
春 (chūn) gives an exact match for 椿's reading.

example.hanzi: 春天,北方人喜欢吃香椿炒鸡蛋。
example.pinyin: Chūntiān, běifāng rén xǐhuan chī xiāngchūn chǎo jīdàn.
example.english: In spring, people in northern China like to eat toon sprouts stir-fried with eggs.
example.fact: Chinese toon sprouts are a prized seasonal delicacy in northern China, available fresh for only a few weeks each spring — their sharp, distinctive aroma makes them a beloved but polarizing ingredient, not unlike cilantro elsewhere in the world.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲫 names the crucian carp.
即 (jí) is close to 鲫's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 鲫鱼汤是一道很滋补的家常菜。
example.pinyin: Jìyú tāng shì yí dào hěn zībǔ de jiācháng cài.
example.english: Crucian carp soup is a very nourishing home-style dish.
example.fact: Crucian carp soup, often made milky-white by pan-frying the fish before simmering, is a classic Chinese postpartum food, traditionally believed to help new mothers produce breast milk and recover strength after childbirth.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锭 names a solid cast piece of metal, an ingot.
定 (dìng) gives an exact match for 锭's reading.

example.hanzi: 古代的银锭常常做成马蹄的形状。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài de yíndìng chángcháng zuò chéng mǎtí de xíngzhuàng.
example.english: Ancient silver ingots were often shaped like horseshoes.
example.fact: Traditional Chinese silver ingots, often called 'sycee' in English, were commonly cast in a distinctive boat or horseshoe shape and served as a major form of currency for centuries before standardized coinage and paper money took over.

components.note: ⺳ (net) — 罔 relates to being caught or covered, as in being deceived or something being denied.
亡 (wáng) is close to 罔's reading — same base sound, different tone.

example.hanzi: 他对同事的建议置若罔闻。
example.pinyin: Tā duì tóngshì de jiànyì zhìruò wǎngwén.
example.english: He turned a deaf ear to his colleague's suggestions, as if he'd never heard them.
example.fact: 置若罔闻 ('to set aside as if not heard') is a common idiom for deliberately ignoring advice, criticism, or a warning — 罔, meaning 'nothing, none,' contributes the sense that the matter was treated as if it never existed.
